metadata.title: Leveraging quantum computing business applications: a B-SLR approach and future research directions

problem_domains.description: The paper identifies financial modeling and forecasting as a business application area where quantum computing could improve prediction and forecast accuracy.
problem_domains.quote: This review emphasizes business applications of QC, including optimization, cryptography and cybersecurity, machine learning, ﬁnancial modeling and forecasting, supply chain management, healthcare and analytics, and materials design, showing how QC can improve prediction and forecast accuracy, data physicalness, large-scale optimization, and more.

problem_domains.problem: optimizing portfolio management and analysing risk
problem_domains.description: Within the financial sector, organizations are pursuing quantum technology to optimize portfolio management and risk analysis.
problem_domains.quote: From the ﬁnancial sector’s pursuit of using quantum technology for optimizing portfolio management and for analysing risk [8, 22] to those working within the pharmaceutical industry examining the use of quantum technology for enhancing molecular simulation and drug discovery eﬀorts [4, 23], and logistics providers examining the potential for increased eﬃciency through routing and scheduling optimization [9] to public sector organizations preparing for the future implementation of anti-quantum cryptography [7, 20], quantum computing has the potential to transform how businesses will address their ever-changing marketplace competition through the creation of innovative new products and services.

problem_domains.problem: organizational readiness for the adoption of quantum computing
problem_domains.description: The paper highlights that existing reviews do not address how ready organizations are to adopt quantum computing.
problem_domains.quote: organizational readiness for the adoption of quantum computing, the speciﬁc pathway for quantum implementation within individual sectors, and the means to create and deliver strategic value related to quantum computing is not addressed within these reviews.

problem_domains.problem: sector-specific quantum readiness and adoption barriers
problem_domains.description: The study aims to assess sector-specific readiness for quantum adoption, distinguishing NISQ feasibility from fault-tolerant requirements and identifying adoption barriers and timelines.
problem_domains.quote: • To assess sector speciﬁc quantum readiness by explicitly distinguishing NISQ era feasibility from fault tolerant quantum requirements and identifying adoption barriers and indicative timelines.

problem_domains.problem: barriers to implementing quantum computers in business practices
problem_domains.description: The paper investigates technological developments and barriers that affect implementation of quantum computers in business practices and their success.
problem_domains.quote: RQ2: How does quantum computing provide value to organizations today; what are the major technological developments, barriers to implementing quantum computers in business practices and factors that will determine the success or otherwise of quantum computing for companies?

solution_approaches.description: The paper emphasizes that near-term value will come from hybrid quantum-classical configurations that operate within NISQ device limitations.
solution_approaches.quote: Thus near-term value for the time being will come primarily through use of hybrid quantum-classical conﬁgurations and application-speciﬁc algorithms that run within the limitations of devices in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era.

solution_approaches.description: VQEs are cited as NISQ-era algorithms designed with shallow circuits and hybrid optimization loops to be feasible on current noisy hardware.
solution_approaches.quote: variational quantum eigen solvers (VQEs), quantum approximate optimizations of problems (QAOPs), hybrid quantum machine learning (QML) models, and sampling-based tasks have been speciﬁcally developed to work under NISQ-era hardware limitations [3, 6]; speciﬁcally, they are based on shallow (few gates) circuits, error mitigation techniques, and optimization loops (classical solutions) which keep their use technically possible with only hundreds of noisy qubits at the moment.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Computing as a Service for Hybrid Classical Quantum Development (QCSHQD)
solution_approaches.description: The QCSHQD framework conceptualizes quantum computing as a cloud-based complementary resource integrated via abstraction layers and hybrid workflows.
solution_approaches.quote: The Hybrid Classical Quantum integration framework represents a view of Quantum Computing as being integrated into the existing classical ecosystem, while also suggesting that quantum computing will be a cloud-based, complementary computational resource to existing systems through Quantum Computing as a Service for Hybrid Classical Quantum Development (QCSHQD), where the emphasis is on establishing abstraction layers and hybrid workﬂows to reduce barriers to entry through expertise and develop incremental value over time, under the current NISQ limitations.

solution_approaches.description: QPF emphasizes co-design of classical and quantum layers to operationalize quantum parallelism in industrial workflows.
solution_approaches.quote: Additionally, the Quantum Parallelism Framework (QPF) emphasizes the need for the co-design of classical and quantum layers, in order to operationalize quantum parallelism in the context of industrial workﬂows.

solution_approaches.description: QFaaS is proposed as an event-driven, modular model of quantum execution integrated into heterogeneous cloud providers and DevOps practices.
solution_approaches.quote: As such, the Quantum Function-as-a-Service (QFaaS) paradigm represents a model of quantum execution as an event-driven and modular architecture that is interchanged and integrated through heterogeneous Cloud-computing providers, while complying with existing DevOps and orchestration best practices.

solution_approaches.description: QKD is presented as a physics-based security model leveraging the no-cloning theorem to establish provably secure communication.
solution_approaches.quote: In particular, the concept of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is an example of this, in that it establishes a provably secure communication model by applying the no-cloning theorem in quantum computing, and by doing so, illustrates the implications to Cybersecurity Governance and Cybersecurity Infrastructure and Compliance Structures.

solution_approaches.approach: hybrid quantum-classical architectures in business applications
solution_approaches.description: The discussion notes that real-world business applications use hybrid architectures where quantum processors handle small tasks within classical workflows.
solution_approaches.quote: Pure quantum solutions were not found in the real world of business by any of the studies. Instead, pure quantum solutions are virtually non-existent in real-world business applications. Hybrid quantum-classical architectures, where quantum processors are used for small deﬁned tasks and integrated into classical workﬂows dominate.

key_claims.claim: Many years or decades remain before large-scale commercial applications using error-corrected, fault-tolerant quantum systems can be built.
key_claims.quote: But for large scale commercial applications of quantum computers using error corrected quantum systems, many years or decades still remain before they can be built.

key_claims.claim: Organizations currently face significant barriers to quantum computing adoption, including underdeveloped technology, lack of skilled labour, integration challenges, unclear regulations, and ROI uncertainty.
key_claims.quote: Organizations are currently faced with signiﬁcant barriers to quantum computing, including underdevelopment in technology, lack of quantum skilled labour, challenges integrating classical information systems using quantum computing principles, lack of clear regulations, and uncertainty surrounding return on investment timing.

key_claims.claim: Existing literature reviews focus on algorithms and hardware but do not address organizational readiness, sector-specific implementation pathways, or strategic value creation for quantum computing.
key_claims.quote: Literature reviews pertaining to quantum computing tend to focus on algorithms and their requirements [5,16,19] through computational complexity, speciﬁc algorithm families, or types of quantum computing hardware architecture. Although each of the reviews is highly regarded within its own respective discipline, organizational readiness for the adoption of quantum computing, the speciﬁc pathway for quantum implementation within individual sectors, and the means to create and deliver strategic value related to quantum computing is not addressed within these reviews.

key_claims.claim: The distinction between NISQ-era and fault-tolerant quantum capabilities is the dominant determinant of near-term business feasibility.
key_claims.quote: Finding 1: the NISQ–fault-tolerant distinction is the dominant determinant of near-term business feasibility

key_claims.claim: Applications like Shor’s algorithm, high-accuracy quantum chemistry simulation, and large-scale QML cannot currently be supported by NISQ hardware because they require millions of logical qubits with full error correction.
key_claims.quote: Alternatively, applications such as Shor’s algorithm (which has a cryptographic signiﬁcance), simulating quantum chemistry with an accuracy of 100%, and large-scale QML require millions of logical qubits with full error correction [11,12]. This means that, based on our synthesis of what’s available, these later types of applications cannot currently be supported by existing or expected NISQ hardware.

key_claims.claim: Quantum readiness is sector-specific and depends on problem structure, digital capability, and willingness to accept experimental uncertainty.
key_claims.quote: Finding 2: quantum readiness is sector speciﬁc and structurally determined There are three observable factors that govern how prepared speciﬁc sectors will be for a transition to quantum computing. These are: (1) The similarity of the problem structure and the types of advantages expected from quantum computing. (2) The ability of the organisation to make digital advancements and have the skills necessary to implement quantum computing; and (3) The willingness of the organisation to willingly accept uncertainty in their experiments.

key_claims.claim: Financial services are relatively prepared for quantum adoption due to potential benefits from NISQ optimization and their financial, technological, and analytical resources.
key_claims.quote: Businesses in the ﬁnancial services sector will also be relatively prepared for a transition to quantum computing due to the potential beneﬁts associated with optimised processes using NISQ algorithms, and because these businesses have adequate ﬁnancial resources, technology and analytical skills to realise those beneﬁts.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing capabilities currently exhibit only partially VRIN characteristics, leading to sustained experimentation without significant commercial deployment.
key_claims.quote: The complementary analysis via Resource Based View (RBV) conﬁrms that at present, quantum computing capabilities display partially VRIN characteristics; they are potentially valuable and rare; but, due to NISQ status, they do not meet the deﬁnitions of inimitability or non-substitutability. As such, these ﬁndings clarify the reasons for the current outcome of sustained experimentation without any signiﬁcant commercial deployment and on-going industry’s development activities.

maturity_indicators.quote: The last decade has seen Quantum Computing grow from mostly theoretical research to a rapidly growing market in both technology and commercial domain.

The current stage of Quantum Computing is known as the NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) stage, which is comprised of Quantum Processors containing anywhere from about 50 physical Qubits up to about 1000 physical Qubits, which have certain limitations due to the high level of restrictions placed upon Quantum Processors by decoherence, gate errors, and limited depth of Quantum Circuits [3,25].

The recent achievements of Google’s Sycamore processor has showcased Quantum Supremacy and the recent advancements in logical qubit stability along with improvements in Quantum Error Correction, as demonstrated by the research of Arute et al. [2] and Acharya et al. [1], conﬁrms considerable progress has been made toward achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing.

From 2004-2012, the scientiﬁc output was comparatively lower than in more recent years, and we attribute this to the developmental stage of quantum computing that was primarily theoretical at this time.
Pure quantum solutions were not found in the real world of business by any of the studies. Instead, pure quantum solutions are virtually non-existent in real-world business applications.

Thus, as organizations look to invest in the near-term future, their investments must be framed as the development of a development capability which generates knowledge, rather than as new applications being ready for implementation.

This study analyzes quantum computing from an organizational standpoint, oﬀering a
comprehensive investigation into the factors that will confer value to organizations at
various stages of quantum technology development.
